blocks.text: “Don't say yes,” answers Miss Smallweed. “I know what you girls are like. Do it without saying it, and then I may begin to believe you.”

Charley swallows a big mouthful of tea to show that she obeys. She clears away the Druid-like ruins of bread and butter so fast that Miss Smallweed orders her not to eat greedily. Eating greedily, Miss Smallweed remarks, is disgusting “in you girls.” Charley might have more trouble satisfying Miss Smallweed's opinions about girls in general, if someone did not knock at the door just then.
“See who it is, and don't chew when you open it!” cries Judy.

Charley, the target of Judy's sharp remarks, leaves the room to open the door. Miss Smallweed uses that chance to push the rest of the bread and butter into a messy pile. She also drops two or three dirty teacups into the low level of tea left in the bowl, like boats into a falling tide. She does this as a hint that she considers the eating and drinking finished.
“Now! Who is it, and what do they want?” says Judy sharply.
It seems to be someone called “Mr. George.” Without any other announcement or polite formality, Mr. George walks in.
“Whew!” says Mr. George. “You are hot in here. Always a fire, eh? Well! Perhaps you are right to get used to one.” Mr. George says this last remark to himself as he nods to Grandfather Smallweed.
“Ho! It's you!” cries the old gentleman. “How do you do? How do you do?”
“Fairly well,” replies Mr. George, sitting down on a chair. “I have had the honour of seeing your granddaughter before. My respects to you, miss.”
“This is my grandson,” says Grandfather Smallweed. “You haven't seen him before. He works in the law, and he is not at home much.”

“My respects to him, too! He is like his sister. He is very like his sister. He is terribly like his sister,” says Mr. George. He puts a strong stress on that last describing word, and he does not altogether mean it as a compliment.
“And how is the world treating you, Mr. George?” Grandfather Smallweed asks, slowly rubbing his legs.
“Pretty much as usual. Like a football.”

He is a dark-skinned, sun-browned man of fifty. He is strongly built and good-looking, with thick, tightly curled dark hair, bright eyes, and a broad chest. His strong, muscular hands are as sunburnt as his face, and they are clearly used to a rather rough life. One curious thing about him is the way he sits forward on his chair. From long habit, he seems to be leaving room for some uniform or military equipment that he has completely stopped wearing. His step, too, is regular and heavy. It would match the heavy clash and ringing sound of riding spurs. He is clean-shaven now, but he holds his mouth as if his upper lip had been used to a big moustache for years. The way he sometimes puts the flat palm of his broad brown hand over his lip gives the same impression. Taking everything together, one might guess that Mr. George was once a horse soldier.

Mr. George makes a striking contrast to the Smallweed family. No horse soldier was ever sent to live with a family more unlike himself. Comparing him to them is like comparing a heavy broadsword to a small knife for opening oysters. His full, strong body contrasts with their small, underdeveloped bodies. His big, open manner, which fills any amount of space, contrasts with their small, narrow, mean ways. His deep, loud voice contrasts with their sharp, thin voices. All these things oppose each other in the strongest and strangest way. He sits in the middle of the gloomy sitting room, leaning forward a little, with his hands on his thighs and his elbows held wide out. Sitting there, he looks as if, by staying long, he would swallow up into himself the whole family and the whole four-roomed house, including even the extra little back kitchen.
“Do you rub your legs to rub life into them?” he asks Grandfather Smallweed, after looking around the room.
“Why, it's partly a habit, Mr. George, and—yes—it partly helps the blood flow,” he replies.
